reference.source: Standard transplantation and haematopathology reference texts
clinicalPearls: A spectrum of lymphoid proliferations arising in the setting of immunosuppression after solid-organ or haematopoietic transplantation
Most cases are driven by Epstein-Barr virus, which transforms B cells that escape control when T-cell immune surveillance is suppressed

The spectrum runs from early polyclonal hyperplasia resembling infectious mononucleosis, through polymorphic disease, to monomorphic lymphoma such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and rarely a classical-Hodgkin-type
Risk is highest in Epstein-Barr-virus-seronegative recipients of a seropositive graft, notably paediatric recipients, and with intense immunosuppression such as T-cell-depleting agents
Presentation is variable, including lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, extranodal masses, allograft dysfunction, and gastrointestinal involvement
A rising Epstein-Barr virus load in the blood can precede or accompany disease and is used for surveillance in high-risk patients
Diagnosis requires tissue biopsy with histology, clonality assessment, and viral studies, with imaging to stage the disease
The cornerstone of treatment is reduction of immunosuppression where feasible, with rituximab for CD20-positive B-cell disease and chemotherapy for aggressive or refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: Immunosuppression weakens cytotoxic T-cell control of Epstein-Barr-virus-infected B cells, allowing latently infected cells to proliferate unchecked. Proliferation is initially polyclonal and potentially reversible, but accumulating genetic changes can drive progression to clonal, autonomous lymphoma. A minority of cases are Epstein-Barr-virus-negative, tend to arise later, and are thought to develop through virus-independent mechanisms related to chronic immune dysregulation.
additionalDifferentials: Primary or reactivated viral infection such as Epstein-Barr virus or cytomegalovirus mononucleosis
Allograft rejection when the presentation is graft dysfunction
De novo or recurrent lymphoma unrelated to transplantation
Other opportunistic infection presenting with lymphadenopathy
additionalInvestigations: Excisional or core tissue biopsy with histopathology, immunophenotyping, and clonality studies
Epstein-Barr-encoded RNA staining of tissue together with blood viral load measurement
Cross-sectional and functional imaging for staging and disease extent
Bone marrow examination where systemic disease is suspected
Lactate dehydrogenase and general laboratory markers of tumour burden
Central nervous system evaluation if neurological involvement is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging masses, B symptoms, or high tumour burden suggesting aggressive monomorphic disease
A very high or rapidly rising Epstein-Barr virus load in a high-risk recipient
reference.prognosis: Early lesions may regress with reduction of immunosuppression, whereas monomorphic and aggressive disease has a worse outlook, although rituximab-based therapy has improved survival; management requires balancing tumour control against the risk of graft rejection.
pitfalls: Failing to consider the diagnosis in any new mass or unexplained illness after transplantation
Not monitoring Epstein-Barr virus load in high-risk seronegative recipients
Allowing avoidable over-immunosuppression that drives the disorder
Treating empirically without a tissue diagnosis and clonality and viral assessment
Reducing immunosuppression without weighing the resulting risk of graft rejection
references: Consensus classification of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders
Transplant immunology and haematopathology reference literature
